title: Rashba-controlled emergence and reversal of critical-field anisotropy in p-wave magnet--superconductor hybrids
authors: Rui-Xiang Cheng, Zhao Gong, Dong-Hui Xu, Chui-Zhen Chen
abstract: We show that tuning Rashba spin-orbit coupling can change the in-plane field direction along which an $s$-wave superconductor is most susceptible to Zeeman depairing. We consider a two-dimensional $s$-wave superconductor subject to an odd-parity exchange field induced by a $p$-wave magnet. Without Rashba coupling, the out-of-plane exchange field enhances the in-plane critical field but leaves its angular response exactly isotropic, despite the anisotropic magnetic spin texture. Minimizing the Bogoliubov--de Gennes grand potential over uniform singlet pairing, we find that increasing Rashba coupling first generates and then reverses the principal-axis critical-field contrast, switching the minimum-critical-field direction by $90^{\circ}$. Equal principal-axis fields at the intervening compensation point coexist with residual angular modulation. We interpret the reversal through competing momentum-dependent depairing contributions from the magnetic and Rashba spin textures, while the on-site singlet pairing channel remains unchanged. Direction-dependent discontinuous collapses of the order parameter further shape the critical-field curves. These results identify a tunable directional paramagnetic response within the uniform-pairing sector. In heterostructures with sufficient electrostatic tunability of interfacial Rashba coupling, this reversal would enable gate control of the easy-depairing axis without reorienting the magnetic texture.
summary: This theoretical work explores how Rashba spin-orbit coupling controls the magnetic field anisotropy in superconductor/magnet hybrids. By tuning the SOC, the paper shows that the direction most susceptible to magnetic depairing can be engineered to reverse by $90^\circ$. This mechanism suggests a pathway for electrically controlling the superconducting response without altering the underlying magnetic texture.
main_problem: The study investigates how tuning Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC) can control the directionality of the critical magnetic field ($H_{c2}$) that depairs an s-wave superconductor within a p-wave magnet hybrid.
main_result: Increasing Rashba coupling first generates, and then reverses, the principal-axis critical-field anisotropy, switching the minimum-critical-field direction by $90^\circ$. This reversal allows for gate control of the easy-depairing axis.
method: The analysis involves minimizing the Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) grand potential over uniform pairing amplitudes to determine the thermodynamically stable superconducting state.
model_or_system: The system is a two-dimensional s-wave superconductor proximity-coupled to a p-wave magnet, modeled using an effective tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating kinetic, p-wave exchange ($h_J$), Rashba SOC ($h_R$), and Zeeman terms ($h_Z$).
key_observables: Critical-field anisotropy ($H_{c2}(	heta)$), principal-axis critical-field contrast ($\eta_{xy}$), and the direction of minimum-critical-field susceptibility.
important_parameters: Rashba SOC strength ($V_R$), p-wave exchange strength ($V_J$), and the magnetic field orientation ($	heta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the uniform pairing sector ($q=0$) and neglects orbital depairing effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual device architecture, the transition from isotropic to $C_2$ anisotropy, and the quantitative reversal of the principal-axis contrast as a function of Rashba coupling strength.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the superconducting state by first establishing the Hamiltonian, then calculating the critical field anisotropy in the pure p-wave limit, and finally demonstrating the tunable reversal of this anisotropy by introducing and varying the Rashba SOC coupling strength.
why_interesting: The ability to tune the superconducting response anisotropy via an external electric field (controlling Rashba SOC) is highly relevant for engineering superconducting spintronic devices and understanding topological superconductivity.
